title: Streamlining a bluff body
summary: Put a flat plate, a cube, a cylinder, a sphere and a streamlined teardrop in the same wind and see where the drag goes: from a drag coefficient above 1 to below 0.1.
objectives: Rank bluff and streamlined shapes by drag coefficient and explain the order with the size of the wake.
Distinguish pressure (form) drag from skin-friction drag and say which dominates for each kind of body.
Recognise a case where the simulation's assumptions (a fully turbulent boundary layer) make it miss the textbook value, and say why.

timeline.what: Objectives; prediction: rank the five shapes by drag coefficient.
Run (or load) the plate, cube and sphere; look at the pressure pictures and the flow slices.
Run (or load) the cylinder and the teardrop; Compare all five.
Explain: wakes, pressure versus friction drag, the sphere miss (drag crisis).

misconceptions: 'A pointed nose is what reduces drag': the tail matters more; a blunt-nosed, pointed-tailed teardrop is a low-drag shape, a pointed-nosed, blunt-tailed one is not.
'Drag is friction': for bluff bodies it is almost all pressure drag from the wake; friction only dominates once the body is streamlined.

'The sphere result is a bug': it is the fully turbulent assumption; the same assumption is why WindLab's drag on wings is high, and the sharp-edged shapes, whose separation is fixed, agree with the handbook.

steps.title: What you will do
steps.text: Five built-in bodies in a 20 m/s wind at zero angle: a flat plate facing the wind, a cube, a cylinder lying across the wind, a sphere and a streamlined teardrop. For bodies the drag coefficient uses the frontal area (the silhouette seen from the front), so the numbers compare directly with textbook tables: about 1.2 for a square plate, 1.05 for a cube, 1.0-1.2 for a long cylinder, 0.47 for a sphere below its drag crisis, and 0.05-0.1 for a good streamlined body.

steps.title: Predict before you run
steps.prompt: Rank the five shapes from highest to lowest drag coefficient (on frontal area) and guess a number for each. Which shape do you expect to have the widest wake? Which the thinnest?

steps.title: Run 1: flat plate
steps.text: A 0.2 x 0.2 m plate square to the wind. Look at the pressure picture: red (Cp near 1) over the whole front, blue behind. In the flow slice, how wide is the slow region behind it?

steps.title: Run 2: cube
steps.text: Same frontal area as the plate. Does the extra depth change the drag much?

steps.title: Run 3: sphere
steps.text: Diameter 0.2 m, Reynolds number 274,000. Where does the flow leave the surface (where does the colour in the slice change from fast to slow)?

steps.title: Observe: the three bluff bodies
steps.prompt: Write down CD for the plate, the cube and the sphere, and describe the wake of each in the flow slice (how wide, how long). Open 'More details': is the drag mostly pressure or friction? (WindLab splits CD into a pressure and a viscous part in the CSV of the mesh study; here judge it from the pictures: a wide dark wake means pressure drag.)

steps.title: Run 4: cylinder across the wind
steps.text: Diameter 0.15 m, three diameters long, with flat ends. This one is hard for a steady solver: the real wake sheds vortices left and right (the Karman street), so the lift trace keeps swinging and the run goes to its iteration limit. Treat its CD as a rough average.

steps.title: Run 5: streamlined teardrop
steps.text: Same frontal area as the sphere, three times as long as it is wide. Compare the wake with the sphere's, then Compare all five runs under My runs.

steps.title: Observe: all five
steps.prompt: Rank the five shapes by CD as WindLab computed them and compare with your prediction and with the textbook values in the introduction. Which shapes agree with the textbook? Which do not?

steps.title: Explain
steps.prompt: Why does the teardrop have roughly a tenth of the sphere's drag with the same frontal area? And why might WindLab's sphere be far below the textbook 0.47?
steps.text: A bluff body's drag is almost all pressure drag: high pressure on the front, low pressure in the wide wake behind where the air could not follow the surface. The plate and cube (CD 1.21 and 1.03 here, textbook 1.2 and 1.05) show it plainly - their skin friction is nearly zero. The teardrop lets the air close in smoothly behind it, so the wake is thin and the pressure recovers; what is left is mostly friction (CD 0.068, half pressure and half friction). The sphere is WindLab's honest miss: it gives 0.25 against the textbook 0.47 at this Reynolds number. WindLab assumes the boundary layer is turbulent everywhere; a turbulent layer clings to the sphere further round before separating, which is exactly what happens to a real sphere only above its drag crisis (Re above about 3 x 10^5), where measured CD does drop to 0.1-0.2. At Re 274,000 a real sphere still has a laminar layer that separates early and a wide wake. The cylinder (0.57) sits between the textbook values for a very long cylinder (1.0-1.2) and a short one with free ends (0.6-0.8), and its lift swings because the real wake is unsteady.

steps.prompt: Which shape has the lowest drag coefficient on frontal area?
steps.explanation: The teardrop: about 0.07 against 0.25 for WindLab's sphere (0.47 textbook) and more than 1 for the plate and the cube. Streamlining means letting the air close in behind the body.

steps.prompt: Where does most of a bluff body's drag come from?
choices: Skin friction on the front face
The pressure difference between the high-pressure front and the low-pressure wake
steps.explanation: On the cube WindLab's viscous (friction) part of CD is essentially zero and the pressure part is 1.03. The wide wake behind a bluff body keeps the rear pressure low; the front is at nearly stagnation pressure.

steps.prompt: WindLab's sphere (CD 0.25) is well below the textbook 0.47. The most likely reason is ...
choices: WindLab's fully turbulent boundary layer stays attached longer, as a real sphere's does only above its drag crisis; at this Reynolds number a real sphere has a laminar layer that separates early
steps.explanation: This is a model limitation, not a mesh problem: the plate and the cube, whose separation is fixed by their sharp edges, agree with the textbook, while the smooth sphere depends on where the boundary layer separates - and that depends on whether it is laminar or turbulent.

steps.title: Homework (optional)
steps.text: Make teardrops with fineness ratios 2, 4, 6 and 8 (diameter 0.2 m) and run each at 20 m/s. Plot CD against fineness ratio: expect a minimum around 3-4, because slim bodies have more surface (friction) and fat ones more pressure drag. Also work out the NACA 0012 wing's drag coefficient on its frontal area from the lift lesson (CD 0.0171 on 0.18 m^2 planform; frontal area 0.036 x 0.6 m) and place it in the ranking.
